title: A theoretical study of taper characteristics to optimize performance
journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
population: Simulation using individual parameters from six subjects of a 15-week training experiment (nonlinear dose-response model)
findings: Without preceding overload, the best simulated performance came with a load reduction of 30.8 +/- 11.8% and duration of 19.3 +/- 2.3 d.
With a preceding 28-day 20% step overload, best performance was significantly higher (P < 0.02) and was reached with a greater load reduction and longer duration (39.3 +/- 9.9% and 28.0 +/- 5.1 d).
A progressive load reduction beat a step reduction only when overload preceded the taper (102.2 +/- 1.7 vs 101.8 +/- 1.5% of steady-state performance, P < 0.005).
Greater training before the taper allows higher gains but demands a greater reduction of load over a longer period; taper adaptations matter in addition to fatigue dissipation.
limitations: Simulation, not an experiment; six subjects' fitted parameters; large between-individual spread; the 28-day optimum after overload exceeds empirical taper durations; no marathon or ultra validation.
implications: Model-based support for scaling taper depth and length with preceding load, as a direction only; do not hard-code simulated values.
Cap taper length at 3 weeks for recreational runners based on empirical data (Smyth & Lawlor, Bosquet).
The between-individual SDs (about 10-12 percentage points in load reduction) argue for allowing individual override.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (MSSE Sep 2005, Thomas first author). Overload was a 20% step increase for 28 d; clarified in findings.
